item.title: The digital solution giving Nigerians a fair chance
item.description:
A locally built digital records system in Nigeria is protecting opportunities and transforming lives by making documents easy to access.

See how real people are shaping progress. Pick a story to begin—or keep scrolling to explore them all.

Faith Obakpolor

Olubayo “Bayo” Adekanmbi

Ero Ugiagbe

Faith Obakpolor once lost a potentially career-changing opportunity because of a missing piece of paper. In 2007, she passed the graduation exam for primary school. Ten years later, when applying for a job with Nigeria’s high court—which required proof of primary school graduation—she learned that her graduation certificate had been destroyed in a fire at her former school. “Oh God,” she remembers the school’s records custodian saying. “We had a fire. All the records we had in the office were destroyed.”  

With no backup copy available, Obakpolor’s only option was to obtain a court-approved testimonial—a process that could take months. By the time she had paid a fee of 10,000 naira (about US$79) for a replacement certificate, the job was no longer available.  

Stories like Obakpolor’s are all too common in Nigeria. The lack of a reliable system to protect and preserve educational records means that every year, thousands of Nigerians lose out on opportunities, hurting their financial prospects and the country’s economic potential. Similar challenges exist in many other parts of the world, where access to opportunities such as education and employment still depend on fragile paper documents. 

The promise of digital public infrastructure 

One solution is digital public infrastructure (DPI): foundational, re-usable digital building blocks—such as digital payments, ID, and data sharing—designed for the public benefit. DPI has the potential to fundamentally transform how individuals access essential documentation and how institutions exchange data, thereby advancing greater economic opportunity and prosperity.  

Nigeria’s Edo State is pilot testing one such tool: EdoCert, a digital system for storing, managing, and providing access to the state’s educational records—at no cost to everyday Nigerians. When Obakpolor, now a secondary school teacher, first heard about EdoCert, she immediately saw its potential to change lives. “I was excited because I realized it meant no other person would go through what I’ve gone through,” she says.  

The instant access to verified educational records that EdoCert provides protects people from costly setbacks like the one Obakpolor experienced. “The problems, the missed opportunities, these are now a thing of the past,” she says. “Generations of kids will no longer face [these obstacles] because they will have a detailed report of their certificates that they can access from anywhere in the world.” 

Quick and easy access to key documents 

Implementing and scaling up a DPI initiative requires deep technical expertise and strategic vision. For EdoCert, these are being provided by Data Science Nigeria (DSN), a nonprofit organization that builds a wide range of data science and artificial intelligence products to improve people’s lives. DSN built EdoCert using Sunbird, an open-source, digital public good from the EkStep Foundation, which will allow the tool to be scaled up for nationwide use.

In a country of nearly 230 million, Nigeria’s educational system still relies heavily on manual recordkeeping. Educational certificates are typically filled out by hand and stored in all kinds of spaces—including closets and storage areas that are susceptible to flood, fire, and rodent infestation. 

...It gives us a practical way to demonstrate how digital public infrastructure can work for the public.

Olubayo “Bayo” Adekanmbi, the CEO of DSN, estimates that in Edo State alone, as many as 1.9 million school certificates exist in paper form only. The resulting challenges are so common that nearly every Nigerian has a story to tell—everything from lost job opportunities to resorting to buying a fake educational certificate. 

Adekanmbi spent several months visiting schools across Edo State to highlight the benefits of digitizing these critical documents. With a technologist’s passion, he spoke with students and educators about everything from the low-cost benefits of EdoCert’s open-source code to its user-friendly interface, which allows people to quickly access their digitized records, including the results of graduation exams. He envisions that the system could be expanded to include other types of documents that provide important verification, such as land registry records and vaccination records. EdoCert is just one example, amongst many, of how DPI can enable new opportunities for all people. “A scalable project like this is so exciting because it gives us a practical way to demonstrate how digital public infrastructure can work for the public,” he says. 

Building trust through verification 

No DPI initiative can succeed without public sector support. Ero Ugiagbe, director of exams for Edo State’s Ministry of Education, sees the value of EdoCert daily. Reliance on fragile paper records and the proliferation of falsified documents have undermined public trust in the government and hampered people’s economic mobility. For too many people, she says, “The trust is not there.” 

Ugiagbe believes EdoCert can help change that. She tells the story of a student she met who had passed the grammar school exam only to have her parents doubt that her paper certificate was genuine. With EdoCert, the truth was quickly revealed: Ugiagbe simply shared a link with the family, and they could see that the exam results were real. “The joy that child had, the smile [on her face] was like, ‘Oh my God, you can see for yourself—that is my result.’ That is a big deal to me,” she says. 

Ugiagbe has been pleasantly surprised to find high levels of public awareness and approval of EdoCert, and not only from teachers and parents. She says, “Even in the market, all the old men and women I speak with are saying, ‘This is good!’” 

Edo State and Adekanmbi's team created radio jingles to promote EdoCert across the state. Listen to the English version or localized Pidgin.

What’s next for EdoCert 

Like Adekanmbi, Ugiagbe sees the potential for broader uses of EdoCert. “Right now, we’re just doing certification, but what keeps me awake [at night] is whether we can do more with demographic data,” she says. “[For instance], I want to know how many female students we have, both in public and private schools. Or the total number of children transferring from one school to another.”  

Collecting this kind of information—in a secure way that protects privacy—could help education officials better track and adapt to changing patterns in school attendance, identify and allocate resources for primary school students that benefit from the national school nutrition program, and support annual resource planning.  

Ugiagbe is also clear that the system isn’t perfect and that challenges remain, particularly the issue of inadequate internet infrastructure in some rural areas. But increasingly, she finds herself telling her counterparts in other states how DPI initiatives like EdoCert can help them serve the public better and more easily. In terms of improving governance, increasing accountability, building trust in public systems, and expanding opportunity, she says, EdoCert “is a dream come true.”

item.title: How one scientist is helping to outsmart the world’s deadliest animal
item.description:
Malaria is one of humanity’s oldest diseases—and one of the deadliest. It kills more than 600,000 people a year, most of them children in Africa under age 5.

Caused by Plasmodium parasites, malaria spreads from person to person through the bites of infected Anopheles mosquitoes, with the heaviest burden falling on young children in sub-Saharan Africa.

Malaria is also preventable and curable. Since 2000, insecticide-treated bed nets have helped prevent over 1 billion cases of malaria in Africa. For families in malaria-endemic communities, a bed net can provide protection and peace of mind while sleeping at night.

But mosquitoes are changing. They’ve been developing resistance to the insecticides traditionally used in bed nets, threatening decades of progress against mosquito-borne diseases. To protect hard-won progress, the world needs new tools to stay ahead of this ancient enemy.

That’s where James Austin comes in. Austin is an American scientist whose team helped create the Interceptor® G2 (IG2), a new kind of mosquito net designed to combat insecticide-resistant mosquitoes and better protect people from malaria.

Meet James Austin

Every morning at his home in North Carolina, Austin enjoys a cup of coffee, the Wall Street Journal, and quality time with Oliver, his 11-year-old goldendoodle. If it’s a nice day, he might sit by the pool and encourage dragonflies to land on his finger. He has loved the outdoors since his childhood in Texas, when he first developed a fascination with bugs.

It’s a serene beginning to a long day that Austin will spend studying—and fighting—the world’s deadliest creatures. As he says, “I’m interested in insects that give us trouble.” For his entire career—in pest control, as a research professor at Texas A&M University, and now as an entomologist in BASF’s Public Health division—Austin has parried with troublesome creatures like termites and Guinea worms. But none have proven more difficult than mosquitoes.

Why mosquitoes have become harder to stop

When Austin arrives at BASF’s offices in North Carolina’s Research Triangle, he usually starts his workday by answering e-mails. Most of his colleagues live and work in Europe, six hours ahead, so he has some catching up to do. But on some days, he goes to BASF’s nearby insect lab to test out a new hypothesis.

When malaria experts sounded the alarm about rising insecticide resistance, Austin and his BASF colleagues were among several private-sector research teams that began working on potential alternatives. “The problem,” he says, “is that the physical chemistry of some insecticides…requires some pretty demanding elements.” For one, they must be water-resistant, so they’ll stay on the net when it is washed. The chemicals must also do two things simultaneously: be deadly to mosquitoes and be safe for kids.

Austin had an idea. Earlier in his career, he helped to develop a pesticide called chlorfenapyr to combat termites. Instead of quickly killing bugs outright like many traditional insecticides, chlorfenapyr kills them slowly, exploiting their metabolism by depleting their energy until they die.

The Interceptor G2: A new way to fight malaria

Working with the Innovative Vector Control Consortium (IVCC), a global health partnership established in 2005 with support from the Gates Foundation, Austin’s team at BASF began developing the IG2, a new net that would include both traditional insecticide and the new chlorfenapyr solution. These efforts gained steam in 2018 with the launch of the New Nets Project, a push by the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, the Gates Foundation, and others to support the development and distribution of nets that could combat rising insecticide resistance.

All insecticide-treated bed nets act as a physical barrier while also killing mosquitoes that land on the net.

Traditional bed nets use a single type of insecticide, pyrethroids, that kills mosquitoes by attacking their nervous system. In many places, mosquitoes have developed resistance to pyrethroids—meaning they don’t work as well as they used to.

The Interceptor G2 net adds chlorfenapyr, which interferes with the mosquitoes’ ability to produce energy. The combination of two insecticides with different modes of action has been the key control aspect.

Put simply, the IG2 uses a double line of attack to target mosquitoes through two mechanisms, with the goal of improving protection against malaria.

While Austin had confidence that the new net would work, its development hit a snag when it came time to test the IG2’s effectiveness. Traditional pesticide testing involves putting mosquitoes in a small, enclosed space, such as a cone, and then coming back in an hour to see how many are dead. But chlorfenapyr takes longer to work. “You just aren’t able to capture the real value of this chemistry with those methods,” he says.

Fortunately, the IG2 showed its true worth in Phase II testing, which involved larger, open spaces and wild, free-flying mosquitoes. “There you could achieve the kind of mortality that is more representative of the chemistry,” Austin says. For example, a two-year randomized trial in Tanzania found that IG2 nets reduced malaria incidence by 45% among kids under age 10 compared with traditional nets.

Protecting families one net at a time

At the end of his workday, Austin heads home to his wife and Oliver, and he often reads a history book or catches up on the latest scientific research.

In the case of chlorfenapyr, the latest research is exciting. item.title: The malaria researcher who won't quit: Dr. Faith Osier
item.description:
“I’m sorry we couldn’t do more.”

As a junior doctor in a rural Kenyan hospital, Dr. Faith Osier often had to look mothers in the eye and say those heartbreaking words. Many children in the pediatric ward died of malaria, sometimes just hours after they had been sitting up and laughing. One by one, the mothers would quietly wrap their child in cloth and begin the long, devastating walk home. “When I look back now, it’s those moments that stayed with me,” Dr. Osier says.

Growing up in a middle-class, urban environment between Nairobi and Mombasa, Dr. Osier was insulated from the scourge of malaria. But beginning her career in that hospital in the Kilifi District opened her eyes. “That’s when the gravity of malaria hit me,” she says. “I would be on the shop floor treating all these patients with malaria and thinking, ‘But if I could just develop a vaccine, then they wouldn’t even come in the first place.’” She was also impressed by the malaria researchers at the hospital who were urgently working to better understand the disease.

Pursuing a research career

Dr. Osier always knew she wanted to go into medicine—like a friend of her mother’s who was a doctor. “For many of us, our careers are shaped by what we see,” she says. “I was lucky enough that there was a female doctor I could look up to.” She later learned that her role model wasn’t just treating patients, she was studying neglected tropical diseases.

But as a young pediatrician, Dr. Osier hardly saw a clear path to becoming a disease researcher herself, given the limited opportunities for female doctors in Kenya to pursue specialist training. Growing up in a middle-class, urban environment between Nairobi and Mombasa, Dr. Osier's world was entirely insulated from the raw devastation of malaria. But that would soon change.

After medical school, she began her career in what was then the Kilifi District in Kenya. “That’s when the gravity of malaria hit me,” she says. There weren't just a few isolated cases of malaria; there was an entire ward of sick children.

Dr. Osier knew she wanted to dedicate her career to fighting malaria to prevent children from dying and families and communities from contracting the deadly disease. She sought out the opportunity to receive specialist clinical training in Kenya and the UK, earning a master’s degree in immunology and a Ph.D. in Life Sciences. In the ensuing years, she has held research, faculty, and scientific leadership positions around the globe, from Australia and Kenya to Germany and the UK, where her posts currently include co-director of Imperial College London’s School of Convergence Science for Health and Technology, and Director of the Imperial Chanjo Hub.

A disease that defies easy answers

“Malaria transmission is different in Africa,” Dr. Osier says, “and it’s because of the geography and climate.”

Malaria is caused by a parasite transmitted to humans by infected mosquitoes. Sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest burden of Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest form of the parasite. Warm temperatures and long rainy seasons create ideal conditions for mosquitoes to breed and thrive, increasing the risk of transmission. In 2024, Africa was home to 95% of the world’s malaria cases and malaria deaths, according to the World Health Organization. The disease claimed 600,000 lives globally that year, three-quarters of them children under age 5. And while geography and climate played a significant role in these numbers, Dr. Osier says that malaria is also a disease of poverty.

“When you go out into the rural areas, some people don’t have decent housing,” she says. “So sometimes you’re giving a [bed] net to someone who doesn’t have a house.” Other factors, like overcrowding, poor sanitation, and poor road construction, create perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes.

The traditional approach to developing vaccines against infectious diseases is rudimentary compared to the complexity of malaria. While many viruses or bacteria have simpler genomes with just a handful of proteins for our immune systems to target, the malaria parasite is more complex with multiple life-cycle stages, its genome encodes thousands of proteins and it has expert ways of evading immunity.

Fortunately, molecular technology has advanced dramatically in recent years. When the first genome of a malaria-causing parasite was published in 2002, researchers finally had a detailed picture of what they were up against. “That’s when we understood,” says Dr. Osier. “We’d been counting maybe 10, 20 proteins. There are actually over 5,000 proteins there. But you couldn’t see them before, because you didn’t have the tools.”

That complexity explains why, even as the malaria field has made meaningful progress, so much remains to be done. Two vaccines, RTS,S and R21, have been approved in the past few years and are reaching children across Africa, but both target just one stage of the parasite’s complex life cycle. Dr. Osier’s work aims to go further, using newer technologies and sophisticated immunological analyses to design a vaccine that targets a different stage, potentially offering stronger and longer-lasting protection.

Life lessons that strengthen resolve

Developing a vaccine can take years, even decades, with obstacles and failures along the way. But Dr. Osier takes the long view. “There are setbacks in work, but there are also setbacks in life,” she says. This has been true in her own life—particularly her experience of enduring multiple miscarriages. “That was a big setback and helped me to appreciate that life happens,” she says. “Life doesn’t respect that you’re a doctor or that you’re researching this great disease. Life is just life, and you must pick yourself up and keep moving every time you fall down.”

Dr. Osier’s scientific approach is to match the complexity of the disease. She started by focusing on an undeniable truth she observed in the rural hospital: The adult wards weren’t full of malaria patients.

“In the exact same house, a child will be at death’s door, but the mom and dad are completely fine,” she says. “That means immunity is possible.”

Understanding how that immunity works has been a yearslong undertaking. “The malaria parasite is like a massive Rubik’s Cube,” she says. “There are millions of bystander antibodies just hanging out, doing nothing. But there are a few that really do the business.”

Her team’s breakthrough advances have come from using cutting-edge protein microarray technology to pinpoint exactly which antibodies are doing the work. That led to several years of work on identifying antigens that were potential vaccine candidates.

When setbacks lead to a new strategy

But then the COVID-19 pandemic hit, hampering Dr. Osier’s research. Even worse, Africa was among the last parts of the world to get access to COVID-19 vaccines, which were developed and manufactured in high-income countries. “During the pandemic, we had vaccine nationalism where rich countries were stockpiling vaccines,” Dr. Osier says. She began to ask herself, “How could I use my knowledge more broadly beyond malaria?” She applied for and was awarded a grant to build vaccine manufacturing capacity in Africa, for multiple diseases.

Dr. Osier’s story underscores a critical truth in global health: The people closest to the problem are the ones best equipped to solve it. She knows this better than anyone. While pursuing her doctorate, she learned about the variability of malaria across the African continent. “Malaria doesn’t have the same face everywhere,” she says, “so when trying to interpret your antibody response, you have to take into account that variability.” She believes strongly in local R&D and equipping local scientists with the skills they need to respond to an epidemic or outbreak in their own community.

Dr. Osier envisions an “army of African scientists” working in concert to advance health innovation across the continent. “You need many people working on the same problem, pushing against each other, and that’s when a solution will emerge,” she says. “We need the Africa to be teeming with scientists.”

item.title: The peer coaching program getting men back on HIV/AIDS treatment in South Africa
item.description:
For Silver Shabalala, the HIV crisis in South Africa hit home in the early 2000s, when he was a goalkeeper with the elite AmaZulu Football Club in Durban. He learned that his brother, imprisoned in Pretoria several hours away, had been diagnosed with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.

“In those days, you were not getting treatment without South African ID,” he says. So Shabalala traveled back to his hometown of Soweto to get his brother’s ID, then brought it to Pretoria to try to get him treatment.

What Shabalala saw at the prison left him heartbroken. “All of these men were sitting there in the corridor, so sick they could not move,” he says. “That day, I made an oath that I would try to understand what HIV is all about.”

Shabalala had already lost other friends and relatives in Soweto to HIV-related illnesses, “but no one spoke about it,” he says. “No one did anything about it. I thought, ‘I cannot lose my brother. I’ll be hands-on. I’ll support him.’”

Why reaching men is a critical gap in the HIV response in South Africa

Shabalala’s family was not alone in being forced to confront HIV. In 2004, at the peak of its toll, HIV claimed about 280,000 lives in South Africa. Thanks to community, government and international efforts, the country’s HIV-related deaths have dropped by 81% since then, and major advances in HIV treatment and service delivery have transformed HIV infection into a manageable chronic condition for many.

Today, roughly one in eight South Africans—or nearly 8 million people—are living with HIV. While women face a disproportionate burden, accounting for twice as many cases as men, men are less likely to know their HIV status, more likely to delay treatment, less likely to stay on treatment, and more likely to die of AIDS and other HIV-related causes. As of March 2023, almost 30% of South African men who knew they were HIV positive were not in treatment.

Shabalala visited his brother often in Pretoria and helped him stay on top of his treatment. When Shabalala retired from professional football (or soccer, as it’s known in the U.S.) in 2007, he knew it was time to do more.

“A lot of football players as well were dying from HIV-related illnesses,” he says. “I needed to start helping my other brothers I was playing with.” As a member of the South African Football Players Union, he pushed for the adoption of an official HIV policy for South Africa’s football players. “I also started getting active and teaching people—current and retired footballers—about HIV,” he says.

Shabalala’s HIV mentoring efforts eventually led him to help launch Coach Mpilo, a remarkably successful peer outreach effort for men living with HIV in South Africa. (Mpilo is a Zulu word meaning life or health.)

You can talk to the coach: A community plan to fight HIV in South Africa

The Coach Mpilo campaign began with a question: Why were so many South African men who were infected with HIV not starting or sticking with treatment?

To learn the answer, Shabalala and his colleagues held workshops across the country and asked the men directly. “They gave us back a simple answer,” he says. “‘Show me a man in South Africa who’s taking treatment, doing well, and is not afraid to speak about it.’ That’s when we understood: A man needs a friend he can speak to, a friend who has walked that journey and has accepted himself. That’s how Coach Mpilo was born.”

Surveys of more than 2,000 South African men confirmed the findings from the workshops. So Shabalala and his colleagues went out to find those HIV-positive friends—“coaches” who could help “players” manage the emotional turbulence that often follows an HIV diagnosis, as well as the logistics involved in finding and continuing with treatment. “Going into a community,” he says, “we look for men who are living comfortably with HIV, have disclosed their condition to their families, and are on treatment. We interview them and then we train them to give them the language that can help men struggling with HIV.”

Shabalala encourages the coaches to use plain language that’s easy to understand. “We like to use examples that men can relate to,” he says. “For example, because a lot of people don’t understand why they need to take treatment, we use B-OK beads in a jar to explain how HIV works in the human body.” This visual aid consists of three small bottles filled with beads—red beads representing the virus and black beads representing healthy cells. Using the bottles, coaches can clearly convey how effective treatment allows people to stay healthy and prevent transmission of the virus to others.

Ultimately, the core virtues of a good coach, Shabalala says, are empathy and vulnerability. “The only way you can connect with another person is to show your own vulnerabilities—to share your own story, your own journey, and your own struggles in life.” Once men start opening up to coaches in one-on-one settings, they come together for group sessions. “For the players, it is very liberating to know ‘I’m not alone,’” says Shabalala.

Getting back in the game: Succeeding against HIV in South Africa

After several years of this outreach across South Africa, the verdict is in: Coach Mpilo has been stunningly successful at encouraging more men to manage their HIV. To date, 96% of the 41,000 men reached by Coach Mpilo have started or resumed treatment. By meeting men where they are, building trust through shared experience, and showing that life with HIV can be healthy and normal with treatment, Coach Mpilo has helped men across South Africa take charge of their health.

Shabalala insists that all credit goes to the coaches. When pressed, he will only concede that “being in the soccer industry helped me to open doors and get the traction going—it makes it easier for men to relate to me and to listen to what I’m trying to achieve.”

Shabalala plans to persevere until every HIV clinic in South Africa has Coach Mpilo coaches that help men stay on target. Unfortunately, deep cuts to public health funding are taking a toll.

“Because of these cuts, some of the coaches are no longer employed,” says Shabalala, “but players are still calling them asking for assistance to go to clinics. Coaches are now helping even when they’re not getting paid. They’re taking players to facilities without transport money and without asking questions. It really shows how the brotherhood we have created with this program is so amazing.”

As for Shabalala’s own brother, he is now out of prison, on top of managing his HIV, and living nearby. “He’s not very far at all now, I see him all the time,” says Shabalala. “He’s got a family. He’s living his life. We can laugh now about the old times and struggles in prison. He’s like, ‘No, no, no. I’m not going back.’”

“The only way you can connect with another person is to show your own vulnerabilities—to share your own story, your own journey, and your own struggles in life.”

item.title: The TB epidemic at a turning point
item.description:
When Sibongile Hlatshwayo began losing weight, it was the first sign that something might be wrong.

Then she started coughing up blood.

Her family rushed her to a nearby clinic. “They couldn’t find anything,” she says, “but I persisted.” After she was transferred to a hospital, doctors ran tests: She tested positive for tuberculosis, or TB. The road ahead was long. “I lost more weight and my body swelled,” she says.

Why a new TB vaccine is needed

The bacteria that cause TB can spread through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks. Active TB can attack the lungs and other parts of the body, like the kidneys or spine. Today, despite decades of medical progress, TB is the world’s deadliest infectious disease. In 2024, an estimated 10.7 million people worldwide became ill with TB. 1.23 million people died from it.

The burden of TB is felt everywhere, but in South Africa, where Hlatshwayo lives, the impact is especially severe, particularly among people infected with HIV. Part of the reason TB remains so difficult to eliminate is that the only available vaccine—which was developed over a century ago—has limited effectiveness in adolescents and adults.

The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, first developed in the early 20th century, is administered to infants all over the world. And while it remains an essential tool for protecting children against the most severe forms of TB, its protection wanes over time and it does not adequately prevent TB in older age groups.

Scientists have worked for decades to develop a vaccine that can protect adolescents and adults, but progress has been slow. Until recently: A vaccine candidate known as M72/AS01E is in Phase III clinical trials across Africa and Indonesia.

Developing a new TB vaccine with African scientific leadership

Dr. Lee Fairlie is a pediatrician and researcher at the University of Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa. She leads a clinical research team at one of the sites involved in the M72 clinical trial, which is sponsored by the Gates Medical Research Institute and funded by the Gates Foundation and Wellcome. As a Phase III trial, the vaccine has been tested for dosage and safety in smaller groups, with early evidence of effectiveness, and is now being evaluated on a larger scale.

If this phase is successful, M72 could become the first TB vaccine to protect adolescents and adult populations around the world.

Dr. Fairlie’s leadership reflects a broader shift in global health innovation. For much of the 20th century, clinical trials in low- and middle-income countries were shaped by institutions outside those regions. Local communities served as research sites but not drivers of the work. That is now changing.

Today, new TB vaccine research in Africa is not only happening on the continent, but it’s also being led, designed, and guided by African scientists across countries including South Africa, Kenya, Malawi, and Zambia.

In South Africa, where more than 56,000 people die annually from TB, the M72 vaccine clinical trial could play a critical role in the effort to eliminate TB.

From prevention to diagnosis, new innovations that could stop TB

The M72 trial is one important piece of a much larger effort to transform how TB is prevented, detected, and treated.

Several other new TB vaccine candidates are advancing in parallel with M72, reflecting renewed investment and momentum in efforts to prevent the disease. At the same time, researchers are also working to strengthen how TB is diagnosed.

Diagnosis remains a major gap in TB response, in part because molecular diagnostic tests—the gold standard—are costly, the samples are difficult to collect, and processing depends on centralized laboratories. New diagnostic tools are portable, use simple tongue swabs, and can be used in primary care settings, and recently received a strong recommendation from the World Health Organization.

Treatments for TB are also evolving. Most patients must still take multiple antibiotics for at least four to six months, even after symptoms disappear. But progress is on the horizon in the form of a new antibiotic named sorfequiline, which was evaluated in combination with other drugs in a Phase II clinical trial carried out at 22 sites. Early results of that trial suggest that a sorfequiline-based regimen could reduce treatment duration. Researchers are hopeful that these outcomes will lead to a Phase III study beginning in 2026.

Taken together, these innovations are changing how experts think about ending TB. Progress will likely come not from a single breakthrough but from a combination of advancements working together: more effective vaccines, faster diagnostic tests, shorter treatments, and health systems that are capable of delivering these tools to the communities that need them most.

The community members shaping TB innovations in South Africa

For six years, Fanyana Ngubane has been advocating for clinical research and infectious disease prevention in South Africa. He believes that the M72 trial speaks volumes about the country’s innovation and ingenuity.

“The country is open to new ideas, to bettering itself, and tackling the challenges that are affecting the community,” he says. This benefits not only South Africans, but people around the world and the entire global health community.

Scientific progress also depends on the relationship between researchers and the communities they serve. Ngubane, a trained member of the M72 trial’s Community Advocacy Board (CAB), helps researchers understand community concerns and ensure that participants’ rights and well-being remain central throughout the research process.

Ngubane and his team hold regular community engagement activities with potential trial participants. Their training prepares them to review consent forms, answer questions, and communicate patient hesitancy to researchers.

“CAB makes sure that the community is informed about the research projects so that there can be ongoing trust between the researchers and the study population,” he says. This continuous feedback from both sides ensures that consent language is clear enough that treatment populations understand what is required of them before they participate in the study. He adds, “Real consent looks like me telling potential participants about all the procedures that are going to be happening. And having them actually explain what I’ve told them back to me.”

These conversations are especially important in settings where historical injustices have contributed to mistrust of clinical research. Across many regions, past experiences, including exploitative research practices and unequal access to medical advances, have left lasting scars. Acknowledging that history is an essential part of building a different future for the research ecosystem.

When ethical oversight, transparency, and community partnership work well, they do more than safeguard study participants. They also improve the quality of the research itself.

The networks of trust built through studies like the M72 trial will continue to shape how future innovations are introduced, evaluated, and shared with communities around the world.

The promise of the M72 vaccine, and a future free of TB

Hlatshwayo was lucky—after six grueling months on TB medication, she was finally free of the disease. But the hope is that one day people won’t get the disease at all.

Breakthrough science is helping to advance TB vaccine development. Diagnostic tools are getting faster and more accessible. Treatment regimens are becoming simpler and easier for patients to navigate.

Across Africa and around the world, scientists, clinicians, community advocates, and global partners are working together to move these advances forward. None of this guarantees immediate success. But with research like the M72/AS01E vaccine trial and sorfequiline, innovation is happening on multiple fronts at once. And many of the people closest to the burden of TB are helping to lead the research that could eventually bring the disease under control.

As the participants arriving each day at research clinics remind us, the search for better tools against TB is not only about science. It is also about people, their health, their families and futures, their tireless pursuit of science and the possibility that the next generation could inherit a world where TB no longer has the power and stigma it has held for so long.

About Tuberculosis

Our goal is to accelerate the global decline in tuberculosis incidence through better vaccines, drugs, and diagnostics.

item.title: What can the world learn from Cabo Verde’s fight against malaria?
item.description:
In 2024, Cabo Verde, an island nation off the coast of West Africa, was certified as malaria-free by the World Health Organization (WHO), meaning it had gone more than three years without a single case of locally transmitted malaria. For a country where malaria was once the leading cause of death, this was a remarkable achievement.  

Adilson DePina, a Ph.D. public health specialist and key researcher and leader in Cabo Verde’s malaria efforts, said his country’s own resources, bolstered with financing from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, “created the backbone” that enabled this success story. The Global Fund is one of the most effective vehicles for advancing progress in health, helping to save an estimated 70 million lives since 2002. 

Alongside this progress against malaria, Cabo Verde has transformed itself economically, rising from low-income to upper-middle-income status. Life expectancy has shot up while child mortality has gone down. And poverty has plummeted. 

Today, 47 countries and territories around the world are certified as malaria-free—and a growing number of others are closing in on elimination. So how did Cabo Verde do it? How is malaria elimination tied with so many other positive ripple effects? Read on and learn about the partnership between the people of Cabo Verde and the Global Fund. 

Lesson 1. Political commitment is crucial to long-term success  

Cabo Verde’s story proves that eliminating malaria isn’t a one-time campaign—it takes sustained leadership and investment over generations. 

DePina says Cabo Verde’s malaria fight stretches back decades. Growing up, he would hear his elders talking about the days when paludismo, as they called the illness in Portuguese, shaped everyday life: “Fevers every rainy season, quinine [medication] lines at clinics, and homes keeping doors shut at dusk.” 

This was the 1940s and 1950s, when malaria was responsible for half of all hospitalizations and was the country’s leading cause of death. Each year, more than 10,000 people became infected. That was about 5% of the population—a huge toll not only on families but on the economy. 

The government, with international help, began concerted malaria-fighting efforts in the 1950s, mostly focused on poisoning mosquitoes and their larvae. In the 1970s and again in the 1980s, the country had several years with no locally acquired malaria cases. Each time, international support fell off and malaria reemerged. The problem was that Cabo Verde lacked the resources to tackle this alone. 

A spate of malaria deaths in 2006 brought the issue back to the forefront. By now, a strong new international organization was fueling momentum against malaria as well as HIV/AIDs and tuberculosis: the Global Fund.  

Lesson 2. Collaboration across sectors is essential 

Eliminating malaria isn’t just a task for the health system. Every part of government, from agriculture to transportation, can play a role when coordination and shared responsibility become the norm. 

Working together, Cabo Verde and the Global Fund developed a plan. Every government agency would play a role. Health officials established treatment protocols. Agricultural officials targeted areas where mosquitoes tended to live and breed. The transportation ministry focused on keeping mosquitoes and disease from arriving at ports. Indoor residual spraying (IRS), which protects people in their homes by spraying walls with insecticide, was stepped up. Campaigns educated residents on what to do—immediately—if they found mosquito breeding sites or experienced malaria symptoms. All malaria testing and treatment would be free. All confirmed cases would be reported to a central database for immediate follow-up, including steps to prevent infections from spreading. 

This collaboration produced results. But then, in late 2017, there was an outbreak, totaling 446 cases. With that setback, the collaborators focused on identifying and addressing gaps. 

Lesson 3. Targeted investments and data can lead to big gains 

When Cabo Verde paired focused investments with better data, the results were transformative. 

Medical entomology technician and researcher Adéritow Gonçalves says that when the outbreak happened, “we didn’t have a lot of information about the mosquito species here, including the density and distribution.” In 2017, the Global Fund worked with the country to open its first medical entomology lab. Now, Gonçalves goes out into the field each week, looking for adult mosquito habitats and breeding sites. With a modern lab, his team is able to track sites and test for insecticide resistance, creating up-to-date malaria transmission profiles for each of the country’s nine inhabited islands. They also help communities identify problem areas and prevent new breeding sites from developing. 

Changing the timing of IRS campaigns also made a big difference after 2017, DePina says.  

“In 2018, we achieved zero locally transmitted cases,” he says. “Now we knew we needed to maintain it.”  

To achieve WHO malaria-free certification, Cabo Verde had to go three years without any indigenous cases and prove that it had everything in place to prevent re-establishment of the disease. It met all the requirements by 2024. By that point, it had been malaria-free for six years. 

All told, the Global Fund malaria investments in Cabo Verde have totaled US$5 million since 2010. That’s about US$10 per resident. Through strong co-financing mechanisms established by the Global Fund, the government has paid for most of the country’s malaria response.  

In just a generation or two, so much has changed. In the 1970s, this nation of islands had only 13 doctors. Today, all of its residents live within 5 kilometers of a government-supported health facility. Childhood vaccination rates are high. The malaria work has led to a stronger health system that is better at identifying and treating other infectious diseases. Cabo Verdeans are living about 20 years longer on average. GDP has increased 12-fold. Is it all connected? 

“I think it’s bidirectional,” DePina says. “Malaria depresses productivity and income. Reducing malaria yields macroeconomic gains while rising incomes and system investment make elimination more feasible.” 

Lesson 4. Stronger health systems build healthier nations 

The effort to end malaria didn’t just stop a disease in Cabo Verde—it strengthened the entire health system. 

Malaria elimination has also helped pave the way for a tourism boom. Some visitors come for the white sand beaches, others explore the mountains, and still others enjoy the city life, all without worrying about contracting malaria. Last year, over a million people visited—a record. Tourism accounts for 20% to 25% of GDP. 

But this also comes with risk. Most visitors are  from nearby countries where malaria is still endemic. If an infected person enters the country, that’s considered an “imported” malaria case. It doesn’t count against WHO certification. However, any imported case can become a new vector for mosquitoes to spread the disease. This can lead to a resurgence of malaria. Cabo Verde has to remain vigilant about tracking all cases while guaranteeing free, accessible treatment.  

It’s not easy. In August, Hurricane Erin threw the country into emergency mode. The storm caused landslides, significant flooding, and, tragically, nine deaths, while also creating more mosquito breeding grounds. 

Not long after, malaria cases began appearing. Vector control at potential mosquito breeding sites has intensified, and health teams are working to protect the population. Under WHO rules, Cabo Verde can keep its malaria-free certification if it quickly stops local transmission and prevents new cases from taking hold—a task that requires strong surveillance and response systems to catch and contain any imported infections. 

Cabo Verde isn’t letting its guard down. This month, the Gates Foundation pledged US$912 million to the Global Fund so the organization can sustain global progress against malaria, HIV, and tuberculosis and continue to protect millions of people. To date, the Global Fund’s partnerships with more than 100 countries have helped cut global malaria deaths by 29%.  

Imagine: If one small island nation can achieve so much, what else can the world achieve in the next 25 years?

item.title: One man’s mission to protect Liberia’s children from polio—one vaccine at a time
item.description:
When polio resurfaced in Liberia after more than a decade, health worker Evans Lablah and his team mobilized a rapid response to stop the outbreak and protect millions of children from the disease.

On a hot and humid morning in February 2021, Evans Lablah, an immunization specialist with UNICEF in Liberia, was working at his desk when he received an email with unexpected news: Variant poliovirus had been detected in the sewage system of Monrovia, the capital city. 

It was a stunning setback. Liberia had been declared free of wild poliovirus 11 years earlier, three years after Lablah got his start in public health in a job overseeing a polio vaccine campaign in a rural district. Since then, the country had routinely tested sewage samples to look for signs of diseases that could be circulating in communities—an important component of a strong public health system. 

The detection of variant poliovirus—a mutated strain of the weakened virus in oral polio vaccine--in the city’s sewage triggered a public health emergency and the formation of a rapid response team to search for the exact source in Monrovia. Lablah, by then a seasoned expert in vaccination campaigns, became part of that team, which included both UNICEF and World Health Organization staff. 

Pursuing a career in health care 

Lablah grew up in Monrovia during Liberia’s 14-year civil war, which lasted from 1989 to 2003. The second of five children, he enjoyed playing soccer and visiting his grandparents in their rural village, where he’d scare away birds from the rice fields and hunt antelope. But it was hard to escape the brutality of living in a war zone. 

By the end of high school, he was desperate to leave the endless fighting. He had always wanted to study medicine, but the war had disrupted training at the country’s two medical colleges.  

In 2001, Lablah received a scholarship to study nursing at a university in Morocco, despite not speaking Arabic or French, the main languages used in education there. He quickly began studying French, and in 2006 he received a nursing degree and returned home. 

Liberia’s health system urgently needed trained workers. More than 95% of its health facilities had been destroyed or damaged in the fighting, and fewer than 20 doctors remained to treat the country’s 3.4 million people. 

Lablah was sent to Grand Cape Mount County, a district in the northwest corner of Liberia whose population of 120,000 was scattered in remote villages. In global health, these are known as “last mile” areas because they are the hardest to reach with health services and are typically underserved.  

Lablah and a midwife were the only trained health workers at one of the district’s five health clinics. They delivered babies and provided primary care services, including routine immunizations, nutritional screening, and maternal health care. Their interaction with patients was often the only contact locals had with the health system. The center lacked just about everything: regular electricity, running water, cellular service, and equipment such as ultrasound machines. Lablah’s US$145 monthly salary barely covered his food expenses. 

  • Learn more

“But as time went by,” he says, “I realized that this was a calling. It was about how I can contribute to humanity and make a difference.” 

In 2007, Lablah became the district coordinator for polio campaigns and led a vaccination team to villages so remote that they had never been visited by a health worker. One of those places was Moila Island, which was an hours long walk from the next village and required stepping across a bunch of logs loosely tied together. In the team’s first attempt to reach the island, the worker carrying the vaccines fell into the water. The team was reluctant to try again, but Lablah reminded them that leaving any pocket unvaccinated would make the country vulnerable to future outbreaks. They returned the next day and vaccinated the 30 children on the island. 

Over the next 15 years, Lablah’s commitment to community health care only deepened. Eventually, he joined the UNICEF Liberia team and began the hard work of strengthening Liberia’s immunization system to protect children from devastating diseases such as measles, polio, pneumonia, and diarrhea.  

This was how he ended up sitting at a desk that day in 2021, staring in shock at the email announcing that polio had been detected in Monrovia’s sewage. 

Polio makes a comeback 

The positive sample came from the sewers of Redemption Ridge, a densely populated neighborhood in Monrovia. The team went to work trying to determine exactly who was infected so they could contain transmission of the virus. 

Poliovirus is spread through contact with human waste, making young children—especially those living in settings that lack clean water and sanitation systems—the most susceptible to exposure. The virus enters the nervous system and can cause permanent paralysis and even death. Most infected people do not show any symptoms, however, so they never know they are infected. This gives the virus time to multiply inside their intestines before being released through their stool. The virus can then spread undetected until there is a case of paralysis, usually in an unvaccinated person, or it’s caught during regular testing of sewage samples. 

The world has been close to eradicating all types of polio for decades. But those efforts have fallen short because of longstanding challenges including low immunization coverage rates, unsanitary living conditions, setbacks related to armed conflict, and weak health systems. 

Lablah and the rest of the rapid response team worked double shifts to investigate the source of the outbreak, and hundreds of other diseases investigators knocked on as many as 100 doors a day, asking residents if anyone in the family had experienced sudden paralysis symptoms.  

“It’s quite a massive undertaking, and the fact that it has to be done immediately when no one is expecting it takes a toll on the delivery of routine health services,” says Lablah. 

The investigation identified two cases of sudden paralysis that had occurred more than 60 days earlier, but the source of the positive sewage sample was never identified. Fifty stool samples collected from healthy children under age 5 in Redemption Ridge all tested negative for the poliovirus.  

A vaccination campaign to stop the outbreak 

An effective rapid response includes a vaccination campaign to cover the outbreak area and those at risk. In Liberia, that meant vaccinating more than 800,000 children over a four-day period one month after detection of the virus, to stop the outbreak from spreading. 

One of the biggest challenges was vaccine hesitancy. One mother was reluctant to vaccinate her 3-year-old son, saying that he had received multiple doses during previous campaigns.  

Lablah explained that the poliovirus can mutate and spread in places where immunity levels aren’t high enough, and that new vaccines had been created to protect against those variants. He also said to her, “If he gets polio, he’s going to be dependent on you for the rest of his life.” He told her that she was healthy because her parents had gotten her vaccinated. The mother decided to have her son vaccinated. 

“I always emphasize to the vaccination teams that they should not just conclude that hesitancy means refusal. When we explain properly why the vaccine is important, it results in the child getting vaccinated,” says Lablah. In Liberia, community and religious leaders are active in the campaigns, listening to concerns and reassuring community members that the vaccines are safe and necessary to protect their children. 

That initial vaccination campaign and a second one in May of that year reached about 1.8 million children—more than 95% of the target age group. 

Forward to eradication 

Since 1988, cases of wild poliovirus worldwide have dropped by 99%. While mutated forms of the virus continue to pop up in a few places around the world, increased surveillance efforts, stronger routine immunization systems, and vaccination campaigns have limited their impact.  

In 2024, Liberia reported another positive sample, prompting supplemental vaccination campaigns. But this time, the campaigns were coordinated with neighboring countries Sierra Leone, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea, and Ivory Coast. As of the first nine months of 2025, Liberia had not detected any poliovirus in sewage samples. Despite the setbacks, Lablah is confident that Liberia—and the rest of the world—will ultimately succeed in eradicating all forms of polio. 

“It’s unacceptable to see success in sight and then give up,” he says. “We just need to be persistent.”
